message.abstract: <ns3:p>Background Education, foreign direct investment (FDI), and trade openness influence environmental sustainability through competing human capital, technology transfer, scale, composition, and pollution-haven channels. Evidence from Sub-Saharan Africa remains fragmented and often overlooks cross-sectional dependence and asymmetric responses. Methods This study examines a panel of Sub-Saharan African economies from 1990 to 2019, using production-based and consumption-based carbon dioxide emissions as environmental outcomes. The empirical strategy applies cross-sectional dependence and slope-heterogeneity diagnostics, second-generation unit root and cointegration tests, dynamic seemingly unrelated regression, continuously updated fully modified and bias-corrected estimators, asymmetric decompositions, and panel causality tests. Results Education is consistently associated with lower emissions across the principal long-run specifications. FDI is associated with lower production-based emissions but higher consumption-based emissions in the principal symmetric estimates, while the asymmetric findings show that the response differs between positive and negative FDI shocks and across time periods. Trade openness is predominantly emission-increasing, and urbanisation is associated with higher emission levels. Robustness analyses support the stability of core associations. Conclusions Sustainability policies in Sub-Saharan Africa should combine environmental education with screening and performance standards for FDI and trade-related production. Policies should consider asymmetric adjustments and economy-specific conditions when pursuing low-carbon development.</ns3:p>
title: Reassessing the Education–FDI–Trade Nexus for a Sustainable Future: Evidence from Sub-Saharan Africa

assertion.value: Md Qamruzzaman; Posted: 28 Aug 2026; Dear Editor and Reviewer, We sincerely thank the reviewer for the constructive and detailed comments. We have revised the manuscript carefully while preserving the original text as much as possible. All changes in the revised manuscript are shown in red ink for convenience. Because the reviewer file repeated the same set of comments, the duplicated comments have been consolidated below and each unique point is answered separately. Comment 1 Reviewer comment: There are numerous grammatical, typographical, and terminology problems that reduce readability. Response: We thank the reviewer for this observation. The manuscript has been carefully edited for grammar, typographical accuracy, terminology consistency, and readability. We also corrected corrupted wording and inconsistent terminology in the introduction, literature review, methods, empirical-results discussion, conclusion, and limitations sections. Manuscript change made: Language and terminology were revised throughout the manuscript. The revisions were made conservatively to preserve the original text as much as possible, and all changes were marked in red ink in the revised manuscript. Comment 2 Reviewer comment: The manuscript states that it investigates Sub-Saharan African economies, while the methods section refers to the 'top 50 polluted nations'. The authors should clearly identify the countries included in the final balanced/unbalanced panel, explain the selection criteria, and report the number of countries and observations. Response: We agree that the earlier wording was inconsistent and could mislead readers about the geographical scope of the study. The manuscript now states clearly that the study concerns Sub-Saharan African economies and that the reported estimation sample is a balanced panel of 50 cross-sectional country units over 1990-2019, yielding 1,500 country-year observations. Manuscript change made: The inconsistent phrase 'top 50 polluted nations' was removed. The data section now reports the 50-country balanced panel, the 1990-2019 period, the 1,500 observations, and the selection criterion based on the availability of the variables required for the final specifications. An author-verification note remains in red requesting insertion of the exact 50 country names and ISO codes from the deposited replication dataset before resubmission. Comment 3 Reviewer comment: Education is described conceptually as educational attainment/human capital, but Table 2 measures EDU as education spending as a share of total government expenditure. These are not equivalent measures. The authors should justify why government education expenditure is an appropriate proxy for education and distinguish expenditure from actual educational attainment, human capital, literacy, or years of schooling. Response: We appreciate this important clarification. The revised manuscript no longer treats government education expenditure as equivalent to educational attainment or realized human capital. Instead, EDU is explicitly presented as a fiscal-input proxy that reflects public commitment to education and the capacity to finance schools, teachers, curricula, and environmental learning. Manuscript change made: Table 2 and the model discussion now define EDU as government education expenditure as a share of total government expenditure. The text explicitly states that EDU is not a direct measure of literacy, years of schooling, education quality, attainment, or realized human capital. The discussion and conclusion were revised accordingly. Comment 4 Reviewer comment: There are important inconsistencies between the reported coefficients and their interpretations. For example, Table 6 reports positive coefficients for EDU and FDI, while the accompanying text interprets these coefficients as reductions in emissions. Response: We agree that the coefficient interpretations needed to be aligned precisely with the reported signs. The empirical-results section has been revised so that each interpretation follows the coefficient signs shown in the corresponding tables and no positive coefficient is described as an emissions reduction. Manuscript change made: The discussion of Tables 6 and 7 was rewritten. The revised text states that EDU and FDI are negatively associated with production-based CO2 emissions in the principal estimates, while trade openness and urbanisation are positively associated with emissions. For consumption-based CO2 emissions, EDU remains negative, while FDI, trade openness, and urbanisation are positive. The abstract and conclusion were also adjusted to reflect these corrected interpretations. Comment 5 Reviewer comment: The authors should explain why positive and negative shocks are expected to have different environmental consequences and clearly distinguish long-run asymmetry from short-run asymmetry. Response: We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion. The revised manuscript now provides a clearer theoretical explanation of asymmetry. It explains that increases and decreases in education expenditure, trade openness, and FDI may have different environmental effects because of adjustment costs, policy responses, sectoral composition, capital-stock adjustment, and technology-transfer channels. Manuscript change made: The asymmetric-model section now explains the decomposition into cumulative positive and negative partial sums. The text distinguishes long-run asymmetry, captured by lagged level terms, from short-run asymmetry, captured by first-difference terms. The interpretation of Table 8 was revised to separate shock direction, time horizon, and emissions-accounting basis. Comment 6 Reviewer comment: The symmetry tests should also be interpreted systematically rather than simply reported. Response: We agree. The revised manuscript now interprets the Wald symmetry tests in a systematic way rather than only listing the statistics. The interpretation identifies which variables show long-run and short-run asymmetry and explains that asymmetry is variable-specific, horizon-specific, and emissions-measure-specific. Manuscript change made: A new explanatory paragraph was added after Table 8. It interprets the Wald tests for EDU, trade openness, and FDI separately for production-based and consumption-based CO2 emissions in both the long run and short run. Comment 7 Reviewer comment: The authors should explain why the selected estimators adequately address reverse causality and omitted-variable bias. If possible, additional robustness checks using alternative specifications or lag structures should be reported. Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s concern. The revised manuscript now explains the role and limits of each estimator more carefully. It clarifies that DSUR, CUP-FM, CUP-BC, CS-ARDL, CCEMG, and AMG address cross-sectional dependence, common factors, dynamic adjustment, and slope heterogeneity, but they do not alone eliminate reverse causality. System-GMM is presented as a complementary robustness check using lagged dependent variables and internal lag instruments. Manuscript change made: The robustness and endogeneity-assessment sections were revised. The System-GMM discussion now reports the interpretation of the lagged dependent variable, AR(1), AR(2), Hansen tests, and instrument counts. The wording was also adjusted to avoid overstating causal identification from an observational panel design. Comment 8 Reviewer comment: The authors should provide a stronger theoretical and empirical justification for the final control-variable specification. Otherwise, omitted-variable bias may affect the estimated coefficients. Response: We agree that the control specification needed clearer justification. The revised manuscript now explains why urbanisation and gross capital formation are included as controls. Urbanisation captures urban scale, density, transport, construction, and energy-demand channels, while gross capital formation captures domestic investment-driven expansion that may affect emissions independently of FDI. Manuscript change made: The methods section now identifies EDU, FDI, and trade openness as focal regressors and urbanisation and gross capital formation as theoretically motivated controls. The text also acknowledges that these controls reduce but cannot eliminate omitted-variable bias because unobserved factors such as energy mix, industrial structure, institutional quality, regulation, and environmental policy may still matter. Comment 9 Reviewer comment: Using both production-based and consumption-based CO2 emissions is a strength of the paper. However, the manuscript should more clearly explain what the differences between these two dependent variables imply for the pollution-haven, pollution-halo, and carbon-leakage arguments. Response: We thank the reviewer for recognizing this strength. The revised manuscript now explains that production-based emissions assign carbon to the territory where production occurs, while consumption-based emissions reallocate embodied carbon to final consumption. This distinction is important because territorial improvements may coexist with imported or consumption-embodied emissions. Manuscript change made: A new discussion was added explaining how the different results for production-based and consumption-based CO2 emissions affect the interpretation of pollution-haven, pollution-halo, and carbon-leakage mechanisms. The revised text avoids a simple pollution-halo conclusion and explains why FDI and trade effects depend on where emissions are accounted for. Comment 10 Reviewer comment: The authors should discuss whether the estimated average effects may conceal substantial country-level differences. Response: We agree. The revised manuscript now states that the reported coefficients are panel-average effects and may conceal substantial country-level heterogeneity in energy mix, institutional quality, sectoral structure, education systems, and environmental regulation. Manuscript change made: A paragraph was added to the empirical discussion explaining the limits of panel-average interpretation. The limitations section was also expanded to recommend future testing of country-level, income-group, sectoral, and embodied-carbon heterogeneity.
